one_liner: The right look, brand new, at four times the price of a scrap unit — and you are gutting something that works.

price.why: ⚠️ By far the most expensive entry here, and the only one where you destroy a working product to do it.

window_w_mm.why: Reissues generally have a small modern display in a period-looking face. Measure before assuming.

chassis.why: Well made, as you would expect at the price.

buttons.why: The reason somebody would consider this at all.

knob.why: Genuinely lovely, and the best-matched knobs to the aesthetic this project is chasing.

display_tech.why: No inverter, nothing charged. Safe to open.

why: The fascia and knobs are period-correct by design rather than by accident, which is the whole aesthetic this project is after.
Brand new, so no broken clips, no faded paint and no missing trim.
Nothing inside is hazardous — modern backlighting, no laser on the mechless ones.
watch_out: ⚠️ You are gutting a working £150–400 product to fit a £30 board. If the look is worth that to you, fine — but be honest that it is a want, not a route to a cheaper deck.
⚠️ Many reissues have a SMALL display in a large face. Measure the window before buying; this is the entry most likely to disappoint on that number.
A reissue that already does Bluetooth, DAB and USB may simply be the product you wanted, without any of this.
steps: Ask honestly whether the unit as sold already does what you want. For several people the correct answer to this entry is 'buy it and stop'.
If not: measure the window before opening anything.
Standard teardown — fascia first, keep every screw.
Nothing inside is charged, so this is a calm strip-down.
Keep the knobs. They are the reason you are here.

models.name: Blaupunkt Bremen SQR 46 DAB
models.note: The reissue of the cult classic, with Bluetooth, DAB and USB built in. ⚠️ Consider buying it and stopping — it may already be the thing you wanted.

models.name: RetroSound Model One / Two and similar
models.note: American, aimed at classic-car restorations, with swappable knobs and faces. ⚠️ Small window in a large face.

models.name: Other 'retro' 1-DIN Bluetooth receivers
models.note: A crowded and inconsistent market. Measure the window from the listing photographs before ordering.

teardown.note: New, undamaged, period-styled. The only reason for this route.
Modern screws, all the same length. A pleasant change.
⚠️ You are binning a working radio. Be at peace with that before you start.

reuse.note: ⚠️ The honest first answer for this family. A modern reissue already does Bluetooth, DAB and USB. Ask whether you want the deck's screens or whether you wanted a nice-looking radio, because if it is the second one you have already bought it.

reuse.value: £12–20 and a part you would otherwise buy
reuse.note: ⚠️ THE BIG ONE. Every CD-era head unit contains a 4-channel amplifier — usually a TDA7388, TDA7850 or similar — already bolted to the chassis as its heatsink and already wired to the ISO speaker connector. That is exactly the part BUILD.md tells you to go and buy. Cut the amp IC's four inputs free of the dead preamp and inject the deck's line out there instead. The IC datasheet gives the pinout; the mute/standby pin usually needs tying to its enable level, and that is the step people miss.

reuse.part: the rear ISO connectors and aerial socket
reuse.value: £8–15 of adapters, and a tidier back panel
reuse.note: The donor's own ISO 10487 A and B blocks and its DIN aerial socket are already mounted in the back panel and already the standard shape. Keeping them means the deck plugs into the car's loom with no adapter and no flying leads out of a hole.

reuse.value: a pound, and some peace of mind
reuse.note: The reverse-polarity diode, the input fuse holder and the filter capacitors on the donor's power input are already rated for a car's supply. Cheap to buy, but they are already there and already fused.
